title: Breaking news
mission: Arc 2 opens with the machinery of news itself: how a fire in the souq becomes a rumor, a bulletin, a statement, a headline, and a correction — and how the anchor's فصحى and the street's عامية tell the same story twice. One story, five retellings. Learn the split once; hear with it forever.
sources: News-register phrasing cross-checked against Al Jazeera Arabic / Wafa bulletin conventions; street forms urban Palestinian koine
Forms cross-checked against Madrasa dictionary and Living Arabic Project (Levantine)
Native-speaker review pending — low-confidence items avoided; uncertain cognates omitted
L6 clip: Raya FM street interviews, embedded from YouTube (never copied)

lessons.title: Did you hear?
lessons.canDo: I can catch a breaking story the way it actually breaks — over the fence, half-confirmed, spreading faster than the smoke.

blocks.body: Unit 4 left you in the souq with change in your pocket. Tonight the souq is on the news. But before any story reaches a screen, it runs through the street's own wire service: a neighbor, a nephew who was passing by, a plume of smoke you can see from the roof. This lesson is that wire service — the words a story wears in its first hour, before anyone official touches it.

example.ar: في خبر عاجل عالتلفزيون — تعالي شوفي.
example.en: There's breaking news on TV — come look.

items.note: خبر عاجل is the red banner that interrupts everything. Same root as Unit 3's مستعجل (in a hurry) — haste, institutionalized.

example.en: A big fire broke out in the vegetable market.

items.note: النار is the flame; الحريق is the event — the thing with a cause, a damage estimate, and a news item.

example.en: Lots of smoke but the fire is small.

cognate.note: n-w-r: Arabic split the root into نار the fire and نور the light; Hebrew kept נר the candle, נורה the bulb, מנורה the lamp — and منارة/מנורה are the same lighthouse. One root, lit at both ends.

example.en: The shop caught fire in an instant.

items.note: The street's fire verb, in both directions: المحل ولع (it caught) and ولع السيجارة (he lit it). The bulletin will say اندلع — hold that thought for Lesson 2.

example.en: The shops closed early today.

items.note: From حلّ — to alight, to settle: a محل is where business settled. File the root; it comes back with a much heavier word in the next unit.

example.en: The fire brigade arrived after a quarter hour.

items.note: From طفى — to put out (Lesson 3 teaches you the verb itself). The ـية makes it the putting-out service.

example.en: The ambulance came fast.

items.note: Literally 'aid-giving' — سيارة إسعاف is the full phrase, الإسعاف does the daily work. الهلال الأحمر, the Red Crescent, is who usually sends it.

example.en: The news spread through the neighborhood before the TV had it.

items.note: Fires and rumors share a verb — انتشر الحريق، انتشرت الإشاعة — and the street's version of both usually wins the race.

example.ar: خسائر كبيرة بالمحلات، بس ولا إصابة.
example.en: Heavy damage to the shops — but not one injury.

items.note: Singular خسارة — which alone is the street's sigh: يا خسارة, what a waste. The news counts خسائر; the street feels the خسارة.

cognate.note: kh-s-r / ḥ-s-r: Arabic خسر loses; Hebrew חסר lacks. After the fire they count الخسائر — literally, what is now missing. Loss and lack: one root, before and after.

example.en: Thank God, no injuries.

items.note: The first question of every breaking story: في إصابات؟ The person is a مصاب. The root also means hitting the mark — أصاب — which is exactly what an injury is, grimly.

blocks.title: Over the wall
blocks.situation: Early evening. Abu Jamil has news; Umm Fadi has questions. Between them, a story assembles itself the way stories actually do — source by source, none of them official.

lines.speaker: أبو جميل
lines.ar: أم فادي! سمعتي شو صار؟
lines.en: Umm Fadi! Did you hear what happened?

lines.speaker: أم فادي
lines.ar: لا، شو؟ خير إن شاء الله؟
lines.en: No — what? Nothing bad, hopefully?

lines.speaker: أبو جميل
lines.ar: في حريق بسوق الخضرة! الدنيا دخان.
lines.en: There's a fire in the vegetable market! Smoke everywhere.

lines.speaker: أم فادي
lines.ar: يا لطيف! مين حكالك؟
lines.en: Good heavens! Who told you?

lines.speaker: أبو جميل
lines.ar: ابن أختي مرق من هناك هلّق. وشفت الإطفائية بحالي.
lines.en: My nephew just passed by there. And I saw the fire truck myself.

lines.speaker: أم فادي
lines.ar: ومحل أبو العبد؟ الله يستر!
lines.en: And Abu al-Abed's shop? God protect us!

lines.speaker: أبو جميل
lines.ar: بقولوا المحلات اللي جنب الفرن ولعوا. بس مش أكيد.
lines.en: They say the shops next to the bakery caught fire. But it's not confirmed.

lines.speaker: أم فادي
lines.ar: في إصابات؟
lines.en: Any injuries?

lines.speaker: أبو جميل
lines.ar: حسب اللي سمعته، لا. بس الخسائر كبيرة.
lines.en: From what I heard, no. But the damage is big.

lines.speaker: أم فادي
lines.ar: طيب افتح التلفزيون — أكيد في خبر عاجل.
lines.en: OK, turn on the TV — there's bound to be breaking news.

questions.prompt: What happened at the market?
Abu Jamil's two sources:
options: ابن أخته، وعينه — شاف الإطفائية بحاله
questions.why: The street's chain of custody: a relative who passed by, plus his own eyes. Note which one he leads with.

questions.prompt: Which shops (allegedly) burned?
Injuries?
questions.why: حسب — Unit 1's sourcing word. A careful speaker staples the source to the claim.

questions.prompt: What is still مش أكيد?
questions.why: بقولوا... بس مش أكيد — the rumor stage: parts of the story arrive before the facts do.

items.en: A big fire broke out in the vegetable market.
The news spread through the neighborhood fast.
The fire brigade arrived after a quarter hour.

points.ar: في حريق — ما في إصابات — صار في
points.explanation: The street reports events with في (there is): في حريق (there's a fire), في إصابات؟ (any injuries?), ما في (there aren't). Push it into the past with كان في (there was) or صار في (there came to be — it broke out). Most breaking news you'll ever hear starts with one of these three, so let your ear lock onto them first.

examples.ar: في دخان كتير عند السوق.
examples.en: There's a lot of smoke by the market.

examples.ar: صار في حريق مبارح بالليل.
examples.en: A fire broke out last night.

points.explanation: The street runs its own attribution system: مين حكالك؟ demands the source; بقولوا (they say) is the anonymous source; سمعت إنه (I heard that) files the claim as hearsay. Unit 1 gave you حسب for quoting properly — these are its street cousins, and speakers grade their own certainty with them. Listen for which one a speaker picks: it tells you how much to believe before they finish the sentence.

examples.ar: بقولوا المحل ولع كله — الله أعلم.
examples.en: They say the shop burned completely — God knows.

examples.ar: سمعت إنه ما في إصابات.
examples.en: I heard there are no injuries.

items.story: n-w-r: the fire-and-light root. Arabic نار burns and نور shines; Hebrew's נר candle, נורה bulb, and מנורה lamp are the same glow domesticated. When the منارة calls and the מנורה burns, it's one ancient filament.

kh-s-r / ḥ-s-r: to lose and to lack. The news tallies خسائر, losses; Hebrew חסר says something is missing. They're the same audit from opposite ends — what you lost is what you now lack. And the street's يا خسارة! is the sound the root makes when it hurts.

lessons.title: The anchor speaks fusha
lessons.canDo: I can tell the anchor's Arabic from the street's Arabic — and translate between them in my head, live.

blocks.body: Here is the secret nobody tells you until it's too late: Arabic is two languages wearing one alphabet. The نشرة is read in الفصحى — the formal standard nobody's mother speaks — while the street answers in العامية you've been learning for four units. Palestinians switch between them without noticing; you're going to learn to hear the switch. Your teacher tonight is a grandfather who has been translating the eight o'clock news back into human speech for fifty years.

example.en: The anchor read the breaking story twice.

items.note: From ذاع — to spread abroad; the مذيع is the spreader-in-chief. Feminine مذيعة. The register he reads in is this lesson's whole subject.

example.en: The six o'clock bulletin is the main one.

items.note: From نشر, to spread — Lesson 1's انتشر is its reflexive sibling. The bulletin is, literally, 'a spreading.'

example.ar: المذيع بحكي بالفصحى، مش زي الناس.
example.en: The anchor speaks fusha — not like people do.

items.note: 'The most eloquent' — the Arabic of bulletins, speeches, and print. Nobody's mother tongue; everybody's news language. You need to hear it, not speak it.

example.en: At home we speak dialect, of course.

items.note: From عام — common, general: the people's Arabic. Also called المحكية, 'the spoken.' It's what this whole app is teaching you — the news is the exception, and that's the point.

example.ar: لهجة أهل الخليل غير عن لهجة نابلس.
example.en: Hebron's dialect is different from Nablus's.

cognate.note: l-h-j / l-h-g: Kohelet sighs that ולהג הרבה יגיעת בשר — much lahag wearies the flesh. That old word for busy talk is Arabic's لهجة, the way a place speaks. What Ecclesiastes waved off, you're now learning on purpose.

example.ar: القناة عاملة بث مباشر من السوق.
example.en: The channel is broadcasting live from the market.

items.note: بث = transmission, مباشر = direct. The street clips it: عالمباشر — on the live. When you hear it, the story is still moving.

example.en: Good evening, dear viewers.

items.note: The anchor's first word to you, every night: مشاهدينا الكرام. From شاهد, to watch/witness — a root with a long memory; its heaviest words are still ahead of you.

example.en: Did you see the report about the fire?

items.note: What Unit 1's مراسل (correspondent) files. The bulletin's building block: خبر then تقرير then مقابلة.

example.en: They interviewed the shop owner.

cognate.note: q-b-l: Arabic قابل is to face — a مقابلة is a face-to-face. Hebrew קיבל is to receive, קבלה the receipt (and the mysticism), מקביל the parallel — what runs face-to-face forever. One root for everything that comes toward you: a guest, a question, a package, the infinite.

example.en: 'Indalaʿa' means 'it caught fire' — got it?

items.note: The hinge of all translation — X يعني Y — and, said alone, the language's #1 filler: يعني... (I mean... well...). You will hear it every eleven seconds for the rest of your life.

cognate.note: Israeli slang borrowed يعني whole — יעני, deployed with the same shrug and the same pause. The little word that translates Arabic to Arabic now moonlights in Hebrew, untranslated.

blocks.title: Grandpa vs. the eight o'clock news
blocks.situation: The bulletin covers yesterday's souq fire. Sido talks back at the television, converting every sentence of فصحى into street Arabic — a free simultaneous-interpretation service he has provided, unrequested, since 1975.

lines.speaker: المذيع
lines.ar: مساء الخير مشاهدينا الكرام. نبدأ نشرتنا بالحريق الذي اندلع مساء أمس في سوق الخضار.
lines.en: Good evening, dear viewers. We begin our bulletin with the fire that broke out yesterday evening in the vegetable market.

lines.speaker: سيدو
lines.ar: اندلع! ليش يا زلمة ما بتقول ولّع زي خلق الله؟
lines.en: 'Indalaʿa'! Why, man, can't you say 'wallaʿ' like God's own people?

lines.speaker: المذيع
lines.ar: وقد سيطرت فرق الإطفاء على النيران بعد ساعتين من اندلاعها.
lines.en: Fire crews brought the flames under control two hours after they broke out.

lines.speaker: سيدو
lines.ar: يعني طفوا النار بعد ساعتين. هيك منقولها إحنا.
lines.en: Meaning: they put the fire out after two hours. That's how WE say it.

lines.speaker: المذيع
lines.ar: ولم تسجل أي إصابات، فيما تقدر الخسائر بعشرات آلاف الشواقل.
lines.en: No injuries were recorded, while losses are estimated at tens of thousands of shekels.

lines.speaker: سيدو
lines.ar: الحمد لله ما في إصابات. بس المصاري راحت — يا خسارة يا أبو العبد.
lines.en: Thank God no injuries. But the money's gone — what a loss, Abu al-Abed.

lines.speaker: المذيع
lines.ar: وقال مصدر في البلدية إن سبب الحريق ما زال مجهولاً حتى الآن.
lines.en: A municipality source said the cause of the fire remains unknown.

lines.speaker: سيدو
lines.ar: يعني بعرفوش ليش ولع. قول هيك من الأول!
lines.en: Meaning: they don't know why it burned. Say so from the start!

lines.speaker: المذيع
lines.ar: وفي الختام، تعود الحياة إلى طبيعتها في السوق صباح اليوم.
lines.en: In closing: life returns to normal in the market this morning.

lines.speaker: سيدو
lines.ar: طبيعتها، الله يعينهم. خلص، خلصت النشرة — طفي التلفزيون يا ستي.
lines.en: 'Normal' — God give them strength. That's it, bulletin's over — turn off the TV, sweetheart.

questions.prompt: The anchor's word for 'caught fire':
questions.why: الفصحى بتقول اندلع؛ الشارع بقول ولّع. Same fire, two dictionaries — this pair IS the lesson.

questions.prompt: How long until the fire was out?
The losses were estimated in…
What does سيدو do with every anchor sentence?
questions.why: يعني... — the grandpa decoder service, free with every bulletin. Your job is to internalize him.

questions.prompt: The cause of the fire, per the bulletin:
questions.why: ما زال مجهولاً — news-speak for 'we don't know yet.' Lesson 4 will get an answer out of them.

items.en: The anchor reads the bulletin in fusha.
At home and on the street we speak dialect.
There's a live broadcast from in front of the market.

items.ar: عملوا ____ مع صاحب المحل اللي ولع.
items.en: They interviewed the owner of the shop that burned.

points.ar: اندلع = ولّع · لا يوجد = ما في · سوف = رح
points.explanation: The decoder ring. Anchor and street run parallel systems, and every news sentence has a street twin: ماذا حدث؟ = شو صار؟ · لا توجد إصابات = ما في إصابات · سوف نعود = رح نرجع · هذا = هاد · الذي = اللي. You don't need to speak فصحى — you need to hear it land and instantly know its twin. That crossing, both directions, is Arc 2's core muscle; this unit onward, every bulletin you meet is practice.

examples.ar: لا توجد إصابات — يعني: ما في إصابات.
examples.en: 'There are no injuries' — meaning: ma fii isabat.

examples.ar: ماذا حدث في السوق؟ — يعني: شو صار بالسوق؟
examples.en: 'What happened in the market?' — meaning: shu sar bis-suq?

points.explanation: Reported speech hangs on إنّه (that): المذيع قال إنه..., جارتي حكتلي إنها... . The فصحى version is قال إنَّ; the street says قال إنه or حكى إنه and suffixes it freely (إنها، إنهم، إنكم). Everything after إنه is a claim, not a fact — the fluent listener hears WHO said before believing WHAT was said. This little word is the hinge of the entire news register; Lesson 4 hangs official statements on it.

examples.ar: المذيع قال إنه ما في إصابات.
examples.en: The anchor said there are no injuries.

examples.ar: جارتي حكتلي إنه المحل ولع كله.
examples.en: My neighbor told me the shop burned completely.

items.story: l-h-j: the busy-talk root. Ecclesiastes filed להג under 'weariness of the flesh'; Arabic promoted لهجة to mean the speech of a place — the very thing you're training your ear on. Two verdicts on human chatter, one root underneath.

The most useful word in this unit crossed the line intact: Israeli Hebrew says יעני — same sound, same shrug, same job of meaning-roughly. When a word for 'meaning' gets borrowed without translation, the joke writes itself.

q-b-l: to face, to receive. An interview is a مقابلة — a facing; a receipt is a קבלה — a receiving; מקביל is parallel — faced forever. From the souq's مقبول (deal accepted) to Friday-night קבלת שבת, one root keeps meeting what arrives.

What سيدو does all bulletin long — بترجم, he translates — is the same four-letter word as Hebrew תרגם, and neither language made it: both inherited Aramaic targum, itself from Akkadian targumannu, the professional interpreter. The Targum translated scripture into Aramaic; the dragoman translated empires to each other; سيدو translates the news to his living room. Oldest job in the region, still hiring.

lessons.title: Eyewitness
lessons.canDo: I can follow an eyewitness telling what happened — in order, in the was-doing tense — and retell the skeleton of it.

blocks.body: The bulletin tells you what happened; the eyewitness tells you what it was LIKE — and does it in a different tense. Where news Arabic stacks masdars, the street narrates: كنت قاعد، سمعت صوت، فجأة... This lesson is the grammar and vocabulary of I-was-there, delivered by the falafel man whose fryer sits twenty meters from where the fire started.

example.ar: حكوا مع شاهد عيان من السوق.
example.en: They talked to an eyewitness from the market.

items.note: Lesson 2's مشاهد watches from the couch; the شاهد عيان watched it happen. Same root, very different evening.

example.en: I saw the smoke with my own eyes.

cognate.note: ʕayn: eye AND spring, the same two meanings on both sides — عين الماء and עין גדי, يا عيني and עין הרע. A root so old it predates the difference between watching and welling up. Every عين on the map is a spring; every one in a sentence is somebody's eye.

example.en: In an instant everything was smoke.

items.note: From لحظ, to glance — a moment is exactly one glance long. Shouted alone — لحظة! — it means hold on!

example.en: Suddenly we heard a loud sound.

items.note: The eyewitness's favorite adverb — it marks the exact seam where the ordinary day tore.

example.en: The sound of the fire truck arrived before it did.

items.note: Sound, voice — and, come Arc 4, the vote: بعطي صوتي، I give my voice. Politics is people sounding off, officially.

example.en: A woman screamed: fire! fire!

cognate.note: ṣ-r-kh: the scream never needed translating — صرخ and צרח, same root, same pitch, same reason to use it. Some words the two languages never bothered to differentiate; panic is one.

example.en: Everyone ran toward the market.

items.note: Note the direction: toward. Where people run when something burns tells you what a حارة is.

example.en: The whole neighborhood scrambled to the fire.

items.note: A beautiful double: فزع is to panic — and to answer the panic. الفزعة is the neighborhood scramble-to-help, an institution with no one-word English translation. You're about to hear one in action.

example.ar: طفوا النار قبل ما توصل الإطفائية.
example.en: They put the fire out before the brigade arrived.

items.note: Lesson 1's إطفائية finally conjugated. Also the TV and the light: طفي الضو. With ولّع you now own both switches — הדליק/כיבה.

example.en: Smoke is still rising from the shop.

items.note: The timestamp particle: لسا بشتغل (still working), لسا ما إجا (hasn't come yet), لسا واصل (only just arrived). Grandmother-in-law-certified since Unit 4: لسا ما أكلت إشي!

blocks.title: I was there
blocks.brief: Abu Samir has fried falafel beside the vegetable market for ten years and has never had a story like this one. Every sentence runs on the was-doing tense — كنت عم، كانوا عم — with فجأة marking the tear. Listen once for the plot, once for the tenses, once for the فزعة.
preQuestions: What was he doing when it started?
Who screamed — and what did the neighborhood do next?
What had already happened by the time the fire brigade arrived?

transcript.speaker: أبو سمير
transcript.ar: أنا محلي جنب سوق الخضرة من عشر سنين.
transcript.en: My shop's been next to the vegetable market for ten years.

transcript.speaker: أبو سمير
transcript.ar: مبارح العصر كنت واقف عم بقلي فلافل زي كل يوم.
transcript.en: Yesterday afternoon I was standing frying falafel like every day.

transcript.speaker: أبو سمير
transcript.ar: فجأة سمعت وحدة عم بتصرخ: حريق! حريق!
transcript.en: Suddenly I heard a woman screaming: fire! fire!

transcript.speaker: أبو سمير
transcript.ar: طلعت بركض — شفت الدخان طالع من محل البهارات.
transcript.en: I ran out — I saw smoke rising from the spice shop.

transcript.speaker: أبو سمير
transcript.ar: الناس كانت عم بتركض من كل صوب، واحد جايب طفاية وواحد جايب مي.
transcript.en: People were running from every direction — one bringing an extinguisher, one bringing water.

transcript.speaker: أبو سمير
transcript.ar: الشباب فزعوا وطفوا نص النار قبل ما توصل الإطفائية.
transcript.en: The guys scrambled and had half the fire out before the brigade arrived.

transcript.speaker: أبو سمير
transcript.ar: لما وصلت الإطفائية، كانت النار لسا بمحلين بس.
transcript.en: By the time the fire truck arrived, the fire was down to just two shops.

transcript.speaker: أبو سمير
transcript.ar: الحمد لله — خسائر بالمصاري، بس ولا إصابة. والفزعة سبقت الدولة، زي دايماً.
transcript.en: Thank God — money was lost, but not one injury. And the neighborhood scramble beat the state, as always.

questions.prompt: What was Abu Samir doing when it started?
questions.why: كنت عم بقلي — the was-doing tense. Hear كان عم and you're inside a flashback.

questions.prompt: How did he learn there was a fire?
Where was the smoke coming from?
Who put out half the fire?
questions.why: الفزعة — the neighborhood's mutual-aid scramble. No dictionary translates it in one word; now you don't need one.

questions.prompt: When the brigade arrived, the fire was…
questions.why: لسا — still/only-just: the little particle that timestamps every scene.

items.en: Suddenly we heard a loud noise.
I saw the smoke with my own eyes.
The whole neighborhood scrambled to the fire.
They put the fire out before the brigade.
The smoke is still rising from the shop.

points.ar: كان عم بِـ... — the was-doing tense
points.explanation: كان + عم + b-verb = was doing: كنت عم بقلي (I was frying), كانوا عم بركضوا (they were running), كانت عم بتصرخ (she was screaming). Arc 1 gave you عم for right-now; add كان and the scene rewinds. This is the tense every testimony, every eyewitness, every 'so there I was' runs on — from here to Arc 3 it will carry the heaviest stories you hear, so let this cheerful fire be your training wheels.

examples.ar: كنت عم بشرب شاي لما سمعت الصوت.
examples.en: I was drinking tea when I heard the sound.

examples.ar: الناس كانت عم بتركض من كل صوب.
examples.en: People were running from every direction.

points.explanation: The storyteller's glue: لما opens the scene (when...), بعدين chains events (then...), قبل ما + verb means before-doing (قبل ما توصل — before it arrived; note: a verb follows, never a noun). Get these three and any narrative snaps into order even when you miss half the words in between — sequence survives vocabulary.

examples.ar: لما شفت الدخان، سكرت المحل بلحظة.
examples.en: When I saw the smoke, I shut the shop in a second.

examples.ar: طفوا النار قبل ما توصل الإطفائية.
examples.en: They put out the fire before the brigade arrived.

items.story: ʕayn: the eye and the spring — both meanings, both languages, unchanged for four thousand years. עין גדי is a spring; عين كارم is a spring; يا عيني and שים עין are eyes. When a root does double duty identically on both sides of the line, you're looking at the family silver.
ṣ-r-kh: scream. Identical root, identical meaning, identical decibels. The proto-Semites clearly needed this word often enough to hand it down intact to everybody.

lessons.title: Confirmed or denied?
lessons.canDo: I can hear an official statement for what it says — and for what it very carefully does not: who confirmed, who denied, according to whom.

blocks.body: Day two: officialdom arrives. News is a chain of custody — مصدر to وكالة to مذيع to you — and every link is held together by two verbs: أكّد (confirmed) and نفى (denied). Today you learn the links, the verbs, and the professional art of saying neither. The spokesman is on the line; count how little he commits to.

example.ar: البلدية أكدت إنه ما في إصابات.
example.en: The municipality confirmed there are no injuries.

items.note: Unit 1's أكيد (for sure), promoted to a verb: to make-sure, out loud, on the record.

example.en: The spokesman denied the report of injuries.

items.note: أكّد's twin — the pair carries half of all news. The same verb also means to exile: pushing away a claim, pushing away a person. Both senses will recur.

example.en: The municipality put out a statement this morning.

items.note: From بان — to become clear. A بيان is officialdom's promise of clarity; grade the promise yourself.

cognate.note: b-y-n: بين is between; a بيان makes things clear — tells them apart. Hebrew בינה is understanding, and הבין is to understand: to tell-between. In both languages, clarity is knowing what stands between what.

example.en: The municipality's spokesman talked to the radio.

items.note: From نطق, to utter — but the full title is the point: الناطق باسم, the one who speaks IN THE NAME OF. Institutions talk through a person; the person is not the source, the باسم is.

example.en: The story is now official — a statement is out.

items.note: From رسم, to draw/inscribe: official means written-down. مش رسمي — unofficial — is where most actual information lives.

cognate.note: r-s-m / r-š-m: Arabic رسم inscribes; Hebrew רשם writes down (רשימה is a list, נרשם is registered). Both languages then agreed: רשמי/رسمي, the official, is whatever got itself written. Bureaucracy's oldest shared axiom.

example.ar: وكالة وفا نقلت الخبر أول وحدة.
example.en: The Wafa agency carried the story first.

items.note: From وكيل, the deputy/agent — an agency acts in your name (there's باسم again). One more life: in refugee-camp speech, الوكالة with no adjective means UNRWA. Context decides.

example.ar: مسؤول كبير حكى إنه التحقيق مستمر.
example.en: A senior official said the investigation continues.

items.note: From سأل, to ask: the مسؤول is the askable one — whoever must answer. Which makes مين المسؤول؟ (who's responsible?) the region's most-asked and least-answered question.

example.en: They opened an investigation into the fire's cause.

items.note: Unit 4 taught you حق — truth, right, price. A تحقيق is truth-work: making-true. And التحقيق مستمر (the investigation continues) is the news' politest way of saying 'stop asking.'

example.ar: شو سبب الحريق؟ لسا مش معروف.
example.en: What caused the fire? Still unknown.

items.note: Every تحقيق hunts a سبب. Plural أسباب — as in لأسباب أمنية, 'for security reasons,' a phrase Unit 6 will teach you to hear a lot.

cognate.note: When medieval Jewish translators — the Ibn Tibbons, rendering Arabic philosophy into Hebrew — needed 'cause' (Arabic سبب), they pressed the root of סבב, to turn, into service: סיבה. The meaning is an Arabic transplant that took so completely nobody feels the seam. Every Israeli סיבה still turns on it.

example.en: The power went out for half an hour yesterday.

items.note: الكهربا comes and goes — راحت وإجت — often enough to be a household member. The suspect in our fire: ماس كهربائي, a short circuit. And Unit 4's كهربجي, the electrician, finally has his subject.

blocks.title: The spokesman commits to nothing
blocks.situation: Morning radio, day two of the fire. The presenter wants answers; the municipality's spokesman has brought a full briefcase of ways not to give any. A masterclass in official Arabic — learn to hear what ISN'T said.

lines.speaker: المذيعة
lines.ar: معنا على الهاتف الناطق الرسمي باسم البلدية. صباح الخير.
lines.en: With us on the line: the official spokesman for the municipality. Good morning.

lines.speaker: الناطق
lines.ar: صباح النور، أهلاً فيكي وبالمستمعين الكرام.
lines.en: Good morning — greetings to you and to our dear listeners.

lines.speaker: المذيعة
lines.ar: نبدأ بالأهم: هل من إصابات؟
lines.en: Let's start with what matters most: are there injuries?

lines.speaker: الناطق
lines.ar: أؤكد لك وللجميع: لا إصابات إطلاقاً، والحمد لله.
lines.en: I confirm to you and to everyone: no injuries whatsoever, thank God.

lines.speaker: المذيعة
lines.ar: هناك من يتحدث عن ماس كهربائي. ما تعليقكم؟
lines.en: Some are talking about a short circuit. Your comment?

lines.speaker: الناطق
lines.ar: التحقيق ما زال مفتوحاً. عند اكتماله، سنصدر بياناً رسمياً.
lines.en: The investigation is still open. Upon its completion, we will issue an official statement.

lines.speaker: المذيعة
lines.ar: يعني لا تؤكدون ولا تنفون؟
lines.en: So you neither confirm nor deny?

lines.speaker: الناطق
lines.ar: أقول إن كل الاحتمالات مفتوحة، والكهرباء واحدة منها.
lines.en: I say that all possibilities are open — and electricity is one of them.

lines.speaker: المذيعة
lines.ar: وأصحاب المحلات؟ الخسائر كبيرة.
lines.en: And the shop owners? The losses are heavy.

lines.speaker: الناطق
lines.ar: البلدية ستقف مع كل من خسر. وهذا وعد — مش حكي جرايد.
lines.en: The municipality will stand with everyone who lost. And that's a promise — not newspaper talk.

questions.prompt: The one thing the spokesman DOES confirm:
On the short-circuit theory, he says:
questions.why: The professional non-answer: neither أكّد nor نفى. You will hear this exact dodge for the rest of your listening life.

questions.prompt: When will there be a بيان رسمي?
حكي جرايد means:
questions.why: 'Newspaper talk' — words with no weight behind them. The street grading the press, in two words.

questions.prompt: Play the word. Who is this?

items.en: The municipality confirmed there are no injuries.
The official denied the report completely.
An official statement came out from the municipality.
Who is responsible for all of this?
They still don't know the fire's cause.
The power was out two hours today.

points.ar: أكّد إنّه — نفى إنّه — لا أكّد ولا نفى
points.explanation: The verdict verbs take Lesson 2's إنه-clause: أكدت البلدية إنه..., نفى الناطق إنه... . Between them lives the official dodge — لا أكد ولا نفى, neither confirmed nor denied — and its cousin كل الاحتمالات مفتوحة. Score every statement you hear against these three boxes: confirmed, denied, dodged. Most land in the third.

examples.ar: البلدية أكدت إنه التحقيق خلص.
examples.en: The municipality confirmed the investigation is done.

examples.ar: المسؤول لا أكد ولا نفى — متل العادة.
examples.en: The official neither confirmed nor denied — as usual.

points.ar: الخبر إللي طلع — المحل إللي ولّع
points.explanation: إللي is the street's only relative pronoun — who, which, that, all of it: المحل إللي ولع (the shop that burned), الخبر إللي سمعته (the news I heard), الناس إللي فزعوا (the people who scrambled). The فصحى splits it into الذي/التي/الذين — you heard the anchor do it — but the street runs everything through إللي. It glues descriptions to things; from now on it's in every third sentence.

examples.ar: المحل إللي ولع رجع فتح اليوم.
examples.en: The shop that burned reopened today.

examples.ar: الخبر إللي سمعته مبارح طلع صحيح.
examples.en: The news I heard yesterday turned out true.

items.story: r-s-m: to inscribe. Arabic رسم draws and prescribes; Hebrew רשם lists and registers. Then both derived the same adjective the same way — رسمي/רשמי, 'written-down' = official. Two bureaucracies, one etymological rubber stamp.

The cause célèbre of borrowed meanings: medieval Hebrew needed Arabic's سبب (cause) to translate Arabic philosophy, so the Tibbonid translators bent סבב — to turn — into סיבה. It took so well that a thousand years later every Israeli 'because' still pivots on an Arabic idea.

b-y-n: from بين, between. Arabic's بيان is a clarification — officially, at least; Hebrew's בינה is understanding itself, and הבין is to tell things apart. Wisdom, both languages agree, is a matter of seeing what stands between.

lessons.title: Headline vs. details
lessons.canDo: I can take a headline apart, find the actual story in the details — and catch the quiet correction when yesterday's version falls apart.

blocks.body: Day three. The fire is out; the coverage is not. Today: the anatomy of a news story — the عنوان that shouts, the تفاصيل that whisper, the تصحيح that mumbles — and the street verb that referees them all: طلع, 'turned out.' Your guide is a young man at the café doing what his generation does to the news: reading it out loud, register by register, and talking back.

example.ar: العنوان أكبر من الخبر، زي دايماً.
example.en: The headline is bigger than the story, as always.

items.note: One word for a headline and a home address — both are where you find the thing. Whether what you find matches the عنوان is this lesson's question.

example.en: Details in the full bulletin.

items.note: Singular تفصيل, from فصل — to separate: details are the story taken apart. The عنوان sells; the تفاصيل tell.

example.ar: أعطيني ملخص — ما عندي وقت للتفاصيل.
example.en: Give me the summary — no time for details.

items.note: The verb is لخّص: لخصلي إياها — give me the short version. What you'll be asked to produce, in English, at the end of every Arc 2 clip. Consider yourself warned.

example.en: A big event — and bigger coverage.

items.note: The thing itself, before anyone writes it up. The root makes حديث (new; talk) and أحداث (events/unrest) — and one very famous Hebrew word; see below.

cognate.note: ḥ-d-th / ḥ-d-sh: Arabic حدث the event, حديث the new; Hebrew חדש new, חודש the new moon, and חדשות — THE NEWS itself. Hebrew literally calls the news 'the new things'; Arabic went with الأخبار, 'the reports.' Two newsrooms, one ancient root — and it's been breaking news since the Bronze Age.

example.en: There are new developments in the fire story.

items.note: تابعوا التطورات — follow the developments: the phrase that keeps a story (and you) refreshing. Singular تطور, evolution/development.

example.en: How's the situation where you are today?

items.note: THE word. كيف الوضع؟ asks about your morning and about the country in the same breath; الأوضاع, plural, is the Situation with a capital S. The purest specimen of the shared register: MSA bones, street soul.

items.en: turned out; came out, went up

example.en: The story turned out to be wrong.

items.note: The street's swiss-army verb — the sun rises (طلعت الشمس), you head out (طلعت من الدار), and above all: the truth surfaces. طلع كذاب — turned out a liar. The people's correction mechanism, no printing required.

example.en: The TV blew the story up, as usual.

items.note: From ضخم, huge: made-huge. The street's standing verdict on coverage — مضخّم — and the exact opposite of what a تصحيح does.

example.en: Every channel covered the fire.

items.note: تغطية = coverage. Same verb as the blanket — غطي حالك, cover yourself, it's cold. One word covers sleepers and stories; judge for yourself which gets tucked in more gently.

example.en: The agency corrected the story a day later.

items.note: Unit 1's صحيح and Unit 4's صحتين, now transitive: to make-true. The تصحيح is journalism's quietest genre — Lesson 6's clip won't have one, but the habit of looking for it should be permanent.

cognate.note: ṣ-ḥ-ḥ: Arabic صحّ is soundness — health (صحة), truth (صحيح), the table blessing (صحتين). Hebrew kept צח for the pure and the clear: צחות is crystalline speech. To correct a story — صحّح — is to restore it to clarity both languages filed under the same root.

blocks.title: Coffee and headlines
blocks.brief: Morning after the statement: a young man at the café reads the fire coverage off his phone — headline voice, then his own. The «quoted» sentences are read as broadcast fusha; everything in between is pure street. One speaker, two registers: the whole unit in one voice.
preQuestions: How many shops actually burned — versus the headline's version of events?
What was the cause in the end, and which register announces it?
His final verdict on headlines vs. corrections — catch the two verbs he lands on.

transcript.speaker: الشب
transcript.ar: «حريق هائل يلتهم سوق الخضار وسط المدينة». هائل! يلتهم!
transcript.en: 'Massive blaze devours the vegetable market downtown.' Massive! Devours!

transcript.speaker: الشب
transcript.ar: يا زلمة، محلين ولعوا. محلين. أنا كنت هناك.
transcript.en: Man, two shops burned. Two. I was there.

transcript.speaker: الشب
transcript.ar: بس العنوان لازم يخوّف — وإلا ما حدا بفتح الخبر.
transcript.en: But the headline has to scare you — or nobody opens the story.

transcript.speaker: الشب
transcript.ar: «التحقيق يرجح أن سبب الحريق ماس كهربائي». هاي معلومة. شكراً.
transcript.en: 'The investigation suggests the cause was a short circuit.' Now THAT's information. Thank you.

transcript.speaker: الشب
transcript.ar: شايف؟ بالتفاصيل الخبر عاقل، وبالعنوان مجنون.
transcript.en: See? In the details the story is sane; in the headline it's insane.

transcript.speaker: الشب
transcript.ar: «البلدية تتعهد بتعويض المتضررين». إن شاء الله — بس هاي سمعناها قبل هيك.
transcript.en: 'The municipality pledges to compensate those affected.' Hopefully — but we've heard that one before.

transcript.speaker: الشب
transcript.ar: وتحت، بخط صغير: «تصحيح: الخسائر أقل من المعلن سابقاً».
transcript.en: And below, in small print: 'Correction: losses lower than previously announced.'

transcript.speaker: الشب
transcript.ar: يعني طلع الخبر نص اللي حكوه. العنوان بصرّخ — والتصحيح بوشوش. هيك الشغلة شغالة.
transcript.en: So the story turned out half what they said. The headline screams — the correction whispers. That's how the machine runs.

questions.prompt: The headline says يلتهم — the reality was:
questions.why: ضخّموا — the gap between العنوان and التفاصيل is exactly this lesson.

questions.prompt: Why must the headline scare, per our commentator?
Where does the story become 'sane'?
questions.why: بالتفاصيل الخبر عاقل وبالعنوان مجنون — frame it and hang it over your feed.

questions.prompt: What arrived in small print?
questions.why: The walk-back: screamed headline, whispered correction. صححوا الخبر — a day late, a font small.

questions.prompt: His closing pair of verbs — the headline… and the correction…
questions.why: Screams and whispers. If you remember one sentence from this unit's meta-lesson, make it this one.

blocks.ttsStyle: Read aloud the following monologue in spoken Palestinian Levantine Arabic — a young man at a café reading news headlines from his phone and reacting to them. Sentences inside «...» guillemets are HEADLINES: read them in formal Modern Standard Arabic broadcast style, clear and measured, like a TV anchor. Everything else is his own sarcastic street commentary: casual, authentic Palestinian dialect (NOT MSA), pronounce إشي as 'ishi'. Speak noticeably slower than natural throughout — calm, learner-friendly pace, clear articulation, small pauses between sentences.

items.en: The headline is bigger than the story.
The details are in the full bulletin, not the headline.
How's the situation there after the fire?
The TV inflated the story — only two shops burned.
The agency corrected the story a day later.
In the end the cause turned out to be a short circuit.

points.explanation: Headlines run on the مصدر — the verbal noun: no tense, no actor, just the event as a thing: اندلاع حريق (outbreak-of-fire), ارتفاع الأسعار (rising-of-prices), إغلاق السوق (closure-of-the-market). The first three seconds of any bulletin are masdar after masdar. Learn to unfold them back into sentences — اندلاع حريق = ولع حريق — and headlines stop being a wall. Warning: the next unit's vocabulary is almost entirely this machine at work.

examples.ar: اندلاع حريق في سوق الخضار وسط المدينة.
examples.en: Outbreak of fire in the vegetable market downtown.

examples.ar: ارتفاع الأسعار قبل العيد.
examples.en: Prices rising ahead of the holiday.

points.explanation: طلع + إنه = it turned out that: طلع الخبر إشاعة (the story turned out a rumor), طلع السبب ماس (the cause turned out electrical), طلع معه حق (he turned out right). Where the paper prints تصحيح in small type, the street says طلع in a loud voice. It's the past tense of the truth: what the facts did once everyone finished talking.

examples.ar: طلع الخبر مضخّم — محلين بس ولعوا.
examples.en: The story turned out inflated — only two shops burned.

examples.ar: طلع أبو العبد منيح، الحمد لله.
examples.en: Abu al-Abed turned out fine, thank God.

items.story: ḥ-d-th / ḥ-d-sh: the crown jewel of this unit's ledger. Arabic حدث (event) and حديث (new); Hebrew חדש (new), חודש (the new moon), חדשות (the news — literally 'the new things'). The two languages built their entire news vocabulary on the same root and never compared notes. Now you have.

ṣ-ḥ-ḥ: soundness and clarity. Arabic صح runs health (صحة), truth (صحيح), table blessings (صحتين), and corrections (صحّح); Hebrew's צח kept the crystalline — pure, radiant, צחות for polished speech. When the agency صححت the story, it did what both languages always meant: made it clear again.

lessons.title: Review & free listening
lessons.canDo: I can follow real street reactions to a real headline — register flips, hedges, and all — and summarize who believes what.

blocks.body: One fire, five retellings: the fence, the bulletin, the eyewitness, the spokesman, the headline. Now the machinery meets reality. Raya FM — an actual Ramallah station — takes a microphone into the street and asks people about the annexation plan that led every bulletin. The reporter asks in news Arabic; the street answers in yours. You will not catch everything. Catch the machinery: who sources, who hedges, who commits. (And keep the topic in your pocket — the next unit is الضفة itself.)

blocks.title: Real street: the mic comes to you
blocks.brief: Raya FM (Ramallah) asks people in the street about the Israeli annexation plan that was leading the bulletins — real voices, real speed, no simplification. The question arrives in news register; the answers come back in street register: the exact split you've spent five lessons training. Two minutes; you own more of it than you think.
preQuestions: Catch the register flip: the framing is news Arabic, the answers are street. Where exactly does each speaker switch?
Score the sourcing and hedging you now know — بقولوا، يمكن، أكيد، والله: how sure is each voice, and how do you know?
Exit ticket: pick ONE speaker and give their opinion in one English sentence. That's the Arc 2 skill, starting now.

items.en: Breaking news: fire in the vegetable market!
The anchor speaks fusha and grandpa speaks dialect.

items.ar: كنت ____ بقلي فلافل لما سمعت الصوت.
items.en: I was frying falafel when I heard the sound.
The spokesman neither confirmed nor denied.
The headline exaggerates — but the details are sane.
In the end the story turned out half what they'd said.
